title: Synthesis routing and cost isolation playbook: multi-tenant QoS and degraded modes
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines a practical, operational approach for routing inference traffic ("synthesis routing") across model variants and capacity tiers while guaranteeing tenant-level quality-of-service (QoS), preserving cost isolation, and providing safe degraded modes when capacity or budget constraints occur. It complements resource-level standards (gpu-node-autoscaling, sharding) by describing routing policies, admission-control knobs, tagging/attribution, and runbook actions.

Scope: Hosted and Dedicated deployments. Private deployments should adopt the patterns here but may vary the enforcement mechanism (local proxies instead of central router).

Motivation

- Customers expect predictable latency and unit cost even during bursts; routing must balance latency SLOs, unit-cost targets, and fairness across tenants.
- Naive global prioritization causes cold-cache starvation and billing surprises; we need explicit admission control plus predictable degraded modes (graceful fallback to cheaper variants) and clear billing attribution.

Goals and non-goals

- Goals:
  - Provide per-tenant QoS classes (gold/silver/bronze + best-effort) mapped to measurable SLOs and throttles.
  - Ensure cost isolation accounting: requests routed under cost-aware policies carry attribution tags and are constrained by token-budget guards.
  - Define deterministic degraded modes with automatic and manual triggers and clear owner escalation.
  - Offer operator playbooks for triage and rollback.
- Non-goals:
  - This playbook does not define low-level kernel scheduling or per-GPU power policies (handled by infra-standards/gpu-node-*).

High-level architecture (textual diagram)

Router components (logical):
  - Edge Proxy: validates auth, enriches context with tenant metadata and QoS class.
  - Synthesis Router: policy engine that computes target model variant and routing tier; applies admission control and tagging.
  - Cost Attributor: attaches cost-centroid metadata (model_id, variant, batch_size, kernel_profile) for billing/observability.
  - Fallback Orchestrator: coordinates canary fallbacks and degraded-mode rollouts.

Sequence on request arrival:
  1) Edge Proxy validates token and resolves tenant_id and tier.
 2) Enriched request forwarded to Synthesis Router with headers: X-Tenant, X-QoS, X-Budget-Id (if present).
 3) Synthesis Router fetches tenant policy + current budgets, evaluates admission control and selects {route_target, reason_code}.
 4) If accepted, tag request and forward to selected runtime pool; if rejected or rate-limited, return standard error with retry-after and suggested cheaper variant.

Policy primitives and terminology

- QoS classes: GOLD, SILVER, BRONZE, BEST_EFFORT.
- Cost band: LOW_COST (quantized/8-bit), MEDIUM (int8/partitioned), HIGH (fp16/fast kernels).
- Admission token: ephemeral per-request token consumed from tenant budget when request is routed to a charged variant.
- Degraded mode: a routing policy state where GOLD->MEDIUM or MEDIUM->LOW_COST is allowed automatically to preserve throughput under capacity pressure.

SLOs and thresholds (example service-level targets)

- Per-tenant p95 latency for GOLD requests: <= 120ms for short-text (<= 512 tokens).
- Per-tenant p95 for SILVER: <= 250ms; BRONZE: <= 500ms; BEST_EFFORT: no strict latency SLO.
- Token budget soft-limit: alert when tenant usage >= 70% of monthly budget; throttle at 100% with configurable fallback.
- Router admission queue depth: default max_queue_ms = 30ms; requests whose expected queue wait > max_queue_ms should be routed to cheaper variant or rejected with 429.

Admission-control algorithm (summary)

1) Compute effective_priority = QoS_weight * tenant_fairness_factor * (1 if within_budget else 0.5).
2) Estimate expectedLatency = baseLatency(route_target) + estimatedQueueWait(tenant).
3) If expectedLatency > qos_slo_threshold(route_target.QoS), attempt cheaper_variant up to 2 levels; if cheaper_variant still violates SLO or budget exhausted, return 429+Retry-After.
4) If budget constraint hits, decrement daily_budget_remaining and emit billing event; if daily_budget_remaining <= 0, mark tenant as budget-exhausted and enforce fallback-only routing.

Configuration matrix (table expressed as fixed-width text)

Parameter | Default | Recommended range | Description
--------- | ------- | ----------------- | -----------
max_queue_ms | 30ms | 10–100ms | Max tolerated router queue wait before seeking cheaper variant
max_batch_size | 32 | 8–128 | Upper bound for batching on target model variant
qos_weights.GOLD | 1.0 | 0.8–1.5 | Multiplicative weight applied to GOLD requests
qos_weights.SILVER | 0.75 | 0.5–1.0 | 
tenant_fairness_decay | 0.95 | 0.5–0.99 | Aging factor to increase priority for long-starved tenants
budget_alert_pct | 70 | 50–90 | Percent of monthly budget to trigger alerts
fallback_levels | 2 | 1–3 | Number of cheaper variants to attempt before rejection

Sample routing policy YAML (example)

policy_id: tenant-route-policy-2026
default_qos: SILVER
routes:
  - name: fast-primary
    cost_band: HIGH
    capacity_tier: reserved
    allowed_qos: [GOLD, SILVER]
  - name: medium-fallback
    cost_band: MEDIUM
    capacity_tier: shared
    allowed_qos: [GOLD, SILVER, BRONZE]
  - name: cheap-degraded
    cost_band: LOW_COST
    capacity_tier: preemptible
    allowed_qos: [BRONZE, BEST_EFFORT]
admission_control:
  max_queue_ms: 30ms
  fallback_levels: 2
  budget_policy: "soft_alert_then_throttle"

CLI examples

- Inspect tenant routing state:
  redwoodctl routing status --tenant t-12345 --verbose
- Force-degrade a tenant to cheap-degraded (operator action):
  redwoodctl routing set-policy --tenant t-12345 --policy cheap-only --reason "ops_{ticket-1123}"
- Query cost attribution for a trace:
  redwoodctl billing trace --trace-id 8f3a2b --show-kernel-metrics

Observability and telemetry

Required metrics (per-tenant / per-route):
- routing.accept_rate, routing.reject_rate, routing.fallback_rate
- routing.p95_latency, routing.p50_latency (tags: tenant, qos, route_target)
- budget.remaining_tokens, budget.pct_used (alert at budget_alert_pct)
- cost.centroid_event -> emits model_id, variant, kernel_profile, batch_size

Required logs: enriched request context including tenant, qos, budget_id, decision_reason, estimated_latency, selected_route. Traces should link router span to runtime span with "X-Routing-Trace-Id" header.

Dashboards and alerts (recommended)

- Tenant QoS overview: per-tenant p95 latency heatmap, fallback_rate.
- Budget saturation alert: fire when budget.pct_used >= 90% for 10m (severity P2).
- Router saturation: routing.reject_rate > 0.5% sustained 5m (severity P1).

Degraded-mode behavior and safe-fail strategies

Automatic triggers:
  - Capacity pressure on HIGH-cost pools (utilization >= 92% for 2m) -> enable degraded mode for SILVER/BRONZE across shared pools.
  - Per-tenant budget-exhausted -> force-fallback to LOW_COST or reject.

Manual operator actions:
  - Evacuate noisy tenant: apply temporary priority decay and move to preemptible pool. CLI: redwoodctl tenant throttle --tenant t-12345 --decay 0.5 --duration 30m.
  - Pause fallbacks during a rollout if quality regressions detected: redwoodctl routing set-flag --name disable-auto-fallback --value true

Quality reviews and guardrails

- Every change to routing policies that affects GOLD or SILVER must have:
  1) A regression test harness with at least 100 synthetic prompts across 3 domains.
  2) A canary rollout (1% traffic -> 5% -> 20%) with automatic rollback on quality or latency regressions.
  3) Observability playbook updated with expected metrics and thresholds.

Rollout checklist (operator playbook)

1) Create policy in staging and run synthetic evaluation.
2) Deploy policy to canary region with 1% traffic. Monitor routing.p95_latency and fallback_rate for 30m.
3) If metrics stable, increase to 5% and run 2-hour smoke tests.
4) If any P1 alerts fire, rollback policy and open incident with "routing-playbook" template.
5) After full rollout, schedule postmortem within 7 days if more than 0.5% of requests experienced fallback.

Troubleshooting quick-reference

- Symptom: sudden spike in fallback_rate for GOLD tenants
  - Check: routing pool utilization, model warm cache hit rates, kernel CPU/GPU stalls.
  - Action: increase reserved capacity for affected model, temporarily reduce qos_weights for non-critical tenants, open infra incident if GPU hot nodes > 85%.
- Symptom: tenant reports unexpected billing increase
  - Check: cost.centroid_event logs for their tenant_id, look for sudden switch to HIGH-cost variants or increased batch sizes.
  - Action: revert recent policy changes, enable tenant budget alerts, notify customer success.

Ownership and governance

- Owners:
  - Routing policy engine: infra-routing team (oncall: infra-routing@pagerduty).
  - Cost attribution and billing hooks: finance-engineering.
  - Observability dashboards: eng-platform observability team.
- Change process: policy changes must follow the ADR process and be recorded in decision-records when they alter core invariants (fairness, billing semantics, or QoS definitions).

Security considerations

- Ensure routing decisions do not leak tenant identifiers in anonymized telemetry exported to third parties. Strip or hash tenant_id before any external reporting.
- Validate that opt-in customer features that route to private variants carry encryption-at-rest and KMS keys consistent with private deployment controls.

Appendix: example incident template (short)

- Title: "Routing fallback surge — region us-west-2"
- Impact window: 2026-02-27 03:12–03:57 UTC
- Symptoms: GOLD p95 latency increased from 95ms -> 310ms; fallback_rate increased from 0.3% -> 9.8%
- Root cause hypothesis: unexpected kernel selector regression causing high tail latency on HIGH-cost pool
- Mitigation steps taken: disabled auto-fallback in region, forced evacuation of problematic nodes, scaled medium-fallback pool by +20% reserved capacity.
- Follow-ups: schedule kernel rollback, update routing health probes to include kernel-latency sensor, run targeted synthetic prompts each deploy.

Related decision records

- When this playbook introduces a new billing-affecting primitive (e.g., "admission token"), an ADR must be created describing the billing contract and migration plan.
